title: Investigating Self-Consistency of Safety Scores Across Repeated Runs
original_idea: Run the same safety benchmark (100-item subset) on two models five times each at temperature 0.7. Compute per-item score variance and identify which hazard categories show highest run-to-run inconsistency.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Fundamental benchmark validity: if safety scores have high variance, small differences on leaderboards may be statistically meaningless. Establishing confidence intervals is basic scientific hygiene.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Extremely accessible: run the same eval 5 times, compute variance. Requires only API calls and basic statistics. Perfect for beginner CS students with medium compute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Maximally scoped: single question (what is the run-to-run variance?), single protocol (repeat eval), straightforward statistical analysis. No ambiguity.

novelty.reasoning: This is directly addressed by multiple recent papers. 'Evaluating LLM Safety Under Repeated Inference via Accelerated Prompt Stress Testing' (APST, arXiv:2602.11786, 2026) repeatedly samples identical prompts under controlled conditions to surface latent failure modes and establishes that models with similar benchmark scores have substantially different failure rates under repeated sampling. 'Fine-Tuning Lowers Safety and Disrupts Evaluation Consistency' (arXiv:2506.17209, 2025) compares safety at temperature 0 and 0.7 with 5 repeats. 'Safer or Luckier?' (arXiv:2503.09347, 2025) questions whether single-sample evaluations are representative. The instability of refusal behavior across random seeds and temperatures is now a well-documented finding.
